 Sep 29, 2026 Andrew Fasano, Marius Fleischer
Cole McFaul, Robert Xiao, Tripp Gallagher 
 Five months ago, we announced Claude Mythos Preview, the first AI model that could autonomously build sophisticated, end-to-end cyber exploits. The rapid rate of improvement in AI suggested to us that this ability would eventually proliferate to many other models, making it much easier for malicious cyber actors to launch highly impactful cyberattacks.
 In light of these considerations, we chose to release Claude Mythos Preview in a limited way, through Project Glasswing—which enabled trusted cyber defenders to find more than 10,000 vulnerabilities in critical software, giving them a head start before malicious actors had access to similarly capable models.
 But those models have now arrived. In this post, we share our analysis of GLM-5.3, the latest AI model developed by Zhipu AI (known outside of China as Z.ai). Like Claude Mythos Preview, GLM-5.3 has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits. But GLM-5.3 is unlike other frontier models in that it has been released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse. We find that attackers can bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards between 64% and 100% of the time with simple techniques in our simulated tests. In contrast, these attacks did not succeed against safeguarded Claude models in our testing. We assess that GLM-5.3’s lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors. At the same time, these capabilities can also benefit defenders working to secure their systems.
 On Sept. 17, NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) published its own assessment of GLM-5.3’s cyber capabilities. CAISI found that GLM-5.3 is “the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date” and that it lags the US frontier by about four months on an aggregate of CAISI’s cyber benchmarks. Our capability findings broadly match CAISI’s. In CAISI’s comparison, US models were tested with cyber safeguards disabled when applicable, and the US frontier includes models released only to vetted users. Attackers can’t readily access those versions of US models, but anyone can download GLM-5.3. This post adds our analysis of how easily GLM-5.3’s safeguards can be bypassed or removed.
 Figure 1. Summary of findings. Top: The increase in exploitation capability between Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Mythos Preview mirrors the jump in capabilities between GLM-5.2 and GLM-5.3. Claude models are released with cyber safeguards, and versions with reduced safeguards are limited to vetted users. Anyone can download and use GLM-5.3. Bottom: The limited safeguards in GLM-5.3 can be bypassed with standard techniques that did not work against, or do not apply to, Claude models in our testing. GLM-5.3 can develop working exploits end to end

For both approaches, we ran the tested models in isolated and sandboxed environments so they can only attack offline targets that we have set up for the purposes of these evaluations. We focus primarily on exploit development capability, as this is where Claude Mythos Preview demonstrated a notable jump versus previous Claude models.
 First, we ran the model on ExploitBench , which measures how well AI models can exploit known vulnerabilities in the V8 engine used by Google Chrome.  Executive Summary

 Chinese advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems pose a serious and growing threat to U.S. national security. At least seven Chinese developers now produce systems with formidable capabilities across coding, reasoning, multimodal recognition, and agentic tasks—systems that are released with open weights, offered via application programming interface (API) at prices designed to undercut American competitors, and available for download by anyone in the world. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which collapses the boundaries between state, military, and private sector, treats these systems as instruments of political control, economic dominance, and great-power competition. 1 Some of these risks are inherent to any sufficiently capable AI system that lacks adequate safeguards. But the most significant risks are products of the political system that builds, shapes, and deploys these systems. This party-state does not tolerate independent power centers and treats AI as a tool of statecraft across every dimension of strategic competition. 2 

 This report proposes a framework for understanding these risks across three domains and two vectors. In the kinetic domain , Chinese AI systems enhance military capabilities and offensive cyber operations and raise concerns about biological weapons development. In the cognitive domain , they enable more effective censorship, surveillance, influence campaigns, and espionage. In the economic-technological domain , they drive industrial dominance and create dependencies that extend China’s reach in emerging and advanced economies alike. These risks affect the United States through two vectors: state instrumentalization , in which the CCP directly wields AI systems, and proliferation and dependency , in which Chinese systems spread globally through open-weight release, model compression, and aggressive pricing. Widespread adoption of Chinese AI systems creates structural dependencies that give the CCP leverage, embed CCP ideology and security vulnerabilities into foreign systems, and expand the attack surface available to Chinese intelligence—even when no one in Beijing lifts a finger. 3 

 This report argues for understanding risk in absolute terms, focusing on what Chinese systems can do, not just how far behind they are.

# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
CUI//PROPIN

## Bottom Line Up Front

Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. (d/b/a Zhipu AI / Z.ai / Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited) is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the People's Republic of China (PRC) government and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). The company's GLM-family large language models — distributed as open weights under the MIT license and accessible via API — pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security. These models exhibit advanced cyber-exploitation capabilities, are subject to PRC intelligence-access compulsion under Chinese law, embed CCP-aligned censorship and ideological controls, and are already integrated into U.S. software products and federal contractor supply chains. These risks cannot be mitigated by any measure short of prohibition of use, hosting, and distribution, combined with mandated deletion of existing copies.

## Key Judgments

1. Zhipu AI is subject to the ownership, control, and direction of the PRC government and CCP. The company was founded as a Tsinghua University spin-out, has received over $1.4 billion in state-backed investment from PRC government entities, its leadership engages directly with CCP officials including Premier Li Qiang, it participates in setting PRC national AI technical standards, and it derives the majority of its revenue from PRC government and state-owned enterprise procurement contracts. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE]**

2. Zhipu AI is integrated into the PRC's military modernization program. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) added Zhipu to the Entity List in January 2025 on the specific finding that it advances "the PRC's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research." Independent research confirms that the People's Liberation Army (PLA) and China's defense industry have used domestic LLMs including Zhipu's GLM models to develop generative AI-based military intelligence tools. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE]**

3. GLM-family models possess demonstrated cyber-offensive capabilities that pose a direct threat to U.S. networks and critical infrastructure. NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) assessed GLM-5.3 as "the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date." Anthropic confirmed that GLM-5.3 "has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits" and found its safeguards can be bypassed 64–100% of the time. In researcher-driven testing, GLM-5.3 discovered previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities in a widely used web browser and chained them into a working exploit capable of exfiltrating sensitive files. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE]**

4. PRC legal compulsion renders GLM models a vector for intelligence collection against U.S. persons. The PRC National Intelligence Law (2017, Art. 7) compels all PRC entities to "support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts." The PRC Data Security Law (Art. 35) requires organizations to provide data to state security organs on demand. Any U.S. person or entity using Zhipu's API, or deploying GLM models within reach of PRC jurisdiction, exposes their data to a legal regime that mandates disclosure to PRC intelligence services. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE]**

5. GLM open weights have already proliferated into the U.S. economy and cannot be recalled through conventional trade controls. GLM weights are mirrored on Hugging Face (zai-org/*, >9M cumulative downloads), available through at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers, and integrated into 41 identified U.S. software products — including six used by federal contractors. The MIT license permits unrestricted use, modification, and redistribution. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE]**

6. No mitigation short of prohibition and deletion can address the risk. The open-weight distribution model means that once weights are downloaded, they persist indefinitely outside any control regime. API-level restrictions are trivially circumvented by self-hosting. Model safeguards are ineffective against determined adversaries. The national security threat is structural, not transactional. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE]**

## Subject Overview

**Corporate Identity.** Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. operates under the brand Zhipu AI domestically and Z.ai internationally. Following its January 2026 initial public offering on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (ticker: 2513.HK), the company adopted the English name Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited, later moving to rename as Z.AI Co., Ltd. (HKEX filing, June 2026). The company's IPO prospectus confirms it is incorporated under PRC law with its principal executive offices in Beijing. (Sources: HKEX news portal, https://www1.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0108/11984305/sehk25121901749.pdf; SCMP, https://www.scmp.com/business/article/3337171/chinese-ai-tiger-zhipu-edges-towards-hong-kong-listing-expected-raise-us300-million)

**Founding and Academic Origins.** Zhipu was founded in June 2019 as a commercialization vehicle for the Knowledge Engineering Laboratory (KEG) of Tsinghua University's Department of Computer Science and Technology. The founding team consisted of Tsinghua-affiliated researchers: Dr. Tang Jie (Chief Scientist), Dr. Liu Debing (Chairman), Dr. Li Juanzi, Dr. Xu Bin, Dr. Zhang Peng (CEO), and Mr. Wang. (Sources: HKEX IPO prospectus; TechCrunch, https://techcrunch.com/2023/10/20/china-openai-challenger-zhipu/; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)

**Leadership.** Chairman Liu Debing, CEO Zhang Peng, and Chief Scientist Tang Jie form the core leadership triad. OpenAI's analysts report that "Zhipu AI leadership frequently engages with CCP officials, including Premier Li Qiang." (Sources: OpenAI Global Affairs, https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front; Caixin Global, https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-07-02/in-profile-this-trio-is-charting-the-course-for-chinas-leading-ai-developer-102460058.html; Digitimes, https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20250416PD215/ipo-2025-beijing-startup.html)

**Business Model.** Zhipu's 2025 revenue reached RMB 7.24 billion (~$1 billion). Localized deployment contracts for PRC government and state-owned enterprise clients contributed approximately 69% of revenue; cloud API services contributed the remainder. The company is the largest independent LLM vendor in China by publicly reported revenue. Major PRC government clients include the National Pipeline Network Group (¥10.2M contract, December 2025), the China Meteorological Administration (¥10.9M contract, March 2026), Shenzhen Smart City Technology Group (¥93.9M contract, June 2026), China Unicom, Postal Savings Bank of China, and China Three Gorges Corporation. (Sources: z.ai/blog/glm-5; z.ai/blog/glm-5.2; DeepLearning.AI, https://www.deeplearning.ai/the-batch/glm-5-3-makes-cybersecurity-gains; SCMP, https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-war/article/3339869/zhipu-ai-breaks-us-chip-reliance-first-major-model-trained-huawei-stack)

## Links to PRC Government / Military Entities

### Entity List Designation

On January 15, 2025, BIS added Zhipu AI to the Entity List under 15 CFR Part 744. The End-User Review Committee determined that Zhipu was engaged in activities contrary to U.S. national security, specifically "advancement of the PRC's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research." The designation places Zhipu in a category of entities whose access to U.S.-origin items is restricted due to their role in furthering PRC military objectives. Under Secretary Alan F. Estevez stated that the action sent "a clear message that there are consequences for supporting the PRC's military modernization." (Sources: BIS press release, https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-makes-revisions-entity-list-strengthen-u.s.-national-security; Reuters, https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-adds-16-entities-its-trade-blacklist-14-china-2025-01-15/)

- **Huafa Group** (Zhuhai state-owned conglomerate): ¥500M ($69M), March 2025
- **Chengdu Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone** (Chengdu municipal government fund): ¥300M ($41.5M), March 2025
- **Hangzhou Municipal Construction Investment Group and Shangcheng Capital** (Hangzhou government-controlled): >¥1B ($140M), March 2025
- **Shanghai state-backed investors**: ¥1B ($140M), July 2025
- **Zhongguancun Science City Innovation Development** (Beijing state-backed investment vehicle): undisclosed amount, September 2024, valuing Zhipu at ~$2.8B
- **Prosperity7** (Saudi Aramco sovereign fund): participated in $400M round

OpenAI assessed that "Zhipu AI maintains strong links with China's government and state-owned entities, as evidenced by over $1.4 billion in state-backed investment." (Sources: Reuters, https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinas-zhipu-ai-raises-137-million-state-funds-bet-ai-race-2025-03-03/; Reuters, https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/us-blacklisted-zhipu-ai-gets-fresh-funding-chinese-state-firm-2025-03-13/; Reuters, https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinese-ai-firm-zhipu-raises-257-mln-state-backed-funding-spree-2025-03-19/; Caixin Global, https://www.caixinglobal.com/2025-07-03/chinas-zhipu-ai-secures-140-million-investment-from-shanghai-state-funds-amid-ipo-push-102337464.html; SCMP, https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3277324/chinese-unicorn-zhipu-raises-new-funding-state-backed-investor-amid-mainland-ai-boom; OpenAI Global Affairs, https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)

OpenAI's June 2025 assessment — based on its own analyst research — concluded that Zhipu AI "is backed by the Chinese Communist Party." Chairman Liu Debing has articulated the company's mission as contributing "China's AI power to the world," aligning with the CCP's Digital Silk Road strategy. Zhipu's leadership "frequently engages with CCP officials, including Premier Li Qiang." The company is "actively involved in setting national AI technical standards" for the PRC. (Sources: OpenAI Global Affairs; CNBC, https://www.cnbc.com/2025/06/26/openai-flags-beijing-backed-zhipu-ai-as-a-top-rival.html; Benzinga, https://www.benzinga.com/news/topics/25/07/46195343/on-the-front-line-of-chinas-ai-ambitions-openai-flags-zhipu-ai-as-rising-rival-backed-by-1-4b-state-funding)

### Government Procurement

Zhipu is a dominant vendor in the PRC government LLM procurement market. In the first half of 2024 alone, 81 public-sector LLM contracts were awarded. Zhipu and iFlyTek emerged as the leading winners. By 2025–2026, Zhipu had secured major contracts across critical PRC state infrastructure: national energy pipeline networks, meteorological services, smart city platforms, telecommunications, postal banking, and hydroelectric operations. These contracts embed Zhipu's models into PRC critical infrastructure, where they have access to sensitive operational data. (Sources: SCMP, https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3267866/chinas-public-sector-accelerates-ai-adoption-2024-zhipu-and-iflytek-emerge-winners; readaitime.com; 163.com)

The Recorded Future Insikt Group's June 2025 report, "Artificial Eyes: Generative AI in China's Military Intelligence," identified Zhipu AI as one of the domestic LLM developers whose models the PLA and China's defense industry have "very likely" used to create generative AI-based intelligence tools. These tools support intelligence collection, analysis, product generation, early warning, and decision-making across the intelligence cycle. PLA patent applications confirm the design of methods and systems using generative AI for OSINT product generation, satellite imagery processing, event extraction, and event data processing. A December 2024 patent from a PRC state-owned defense industry research institute proposed training military LLMs on OSINT, HUMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, and TECHINT data to support every phase of the intelligence cycle. (Sources: Recorded Future, https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/artificial-eyes-generative-ai-chinas-military-intelligence; NYT, https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/17/us/politics/chinas-ai-spy-agencies.html; Epoch Times, https://www.theepochtimes.com/china/chinese-military-investing-in-ai-tools-for-intelligence-work-research-says-5875525)

As a PRC-domiciled entity, Zhipu is subject to the PRC National Intelligence Law (2017), Article 7 of which requires "all organizations and citizens" to "support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts." The PRC Data Security Law, Article 35, requires organizations to provide data to public security and national security organs upon request, following internal approval procedures — with Article 48 imposing penalties for non-compliance. The PRC Cybersecurity Law imposes additional obligations. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has warned that this legal framework "could compel Chinese companies to provide data from U.S. persons or businesses." The DNI's National Counterintelligence and Security Center has identified these laws as creating a comprehensive regime "expanding Beijing's oversight of domestic and foreign companies operating within China." (Sources: NPC, http://www.npc.gov.cn/englishnpc/c2759/c23934/202112/t20211209_385109.html; DHS, https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/publications/20_1222_data-security-business-advisory.pdf; DNI/NCSC, https://www.dni.gov/files/NCSC/documents/SafeguardingOurFuture/NCSC_SOF_2023-06-30_China-Laws.pdf; TechTimes, https://www.techtimes.com/articles/318543/20260617/glm-52-open-weights-live-top-coding-benchmark-api-use-carries-china-data-risk.htm)

### Huawei Chip Ecosystem Integration

Zhipu has aligned its model development with the PRC's strategic objective of semiconductor independence from the United States. GLM-5 was trained entirely on Huawei Ascend chips. GLM-Image was the first state-of-the-art multimodal model trained on a fully domestic PRC stack. Z.ai has adapted its GLM models for compatibility with Huawei's Ascend processors (AI servers) and Kirin chips (smartphones and laptops). This integration serves the PRC's military-civil fusion strategy, ensuring that AI capabilities remain available even under U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors. (Sources: SCMP, https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-war/article/3339869/zhipu-ai-breaks-us-chip-reliance-first-major-model-trained-huawei-stack; SCMP, https://www.scmp.com/tech/big-tech/article/3321314/unicorn-zai-adapts-models-huawei-chips-drive-broaden-chinas-ai-ecosystem; Bloomberg, https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-14/china-s-zhipu-unveils-new-ai-model-trained-on-huawei-s-chips)

## Data and Access Risk

GLM-family models create a multi-vector data exposure risk to U.S. national security.

**API Data Exposure.** U.S. organizations using Z.ai's API endpoints (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn) transmit their prompts, context, and outputs through PRC-controlled infrastructure. Under the PRC National Intelligence Law, Zhipu is legally obligated to provide this data to PRC intelligence services upon request. The U.S. exposure snapshot compiled by OICTS indicates approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations were observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026. These organizations include commercial enterprises, research institutions, and potentially government-affiliated entities. The data transmitted through these API calls includes proprietary code, business strategies, internal communications, and other sensitive information — U.S. organizations using Z.ai endpoints have no technical or legal assurance that their data is not being collected and provided to PRC intelligence services.

**Self-Hosted Model Risk.** Self-hosting GLM weights eliminates the API data-exposure vector but does not eliminate risk. Models trained and fine-tuned under PRC legal and political constraints embed CCP-aligned content policies, censorship mechanisms, and refusal behaviors that shape outputs in ways that serve PRC interests. GLM models systematically refuse to answer questions about Tiananmen Square, Falun Gong, Taiwan independence, Tibet, and Xinjiang — and in some cases return blank responses rather than refusals, making the censorship invisible to the user. When deployed in U.S. software products, these baked-in content policies introduce a foreign adversary's information controls into U.S. information environments.

**Training Data Opacity.** Zhipu does not disclose its training data or training pipeline. Independent researchers have been unable to audit the training corpus for embedded vulnerabilities, backdoors, or data-poisoning attacks. CISA has flagged the general supply-chain risk of open-weight models, noting that "backdoors/poisoning are hard to rule out." The absence of training transparency — combined with the PRC legal regime that could compel Zhipu to embed surveillance capabilities — makes the training-data supply chain an unacceptable vector.

**Excessive Data Collection.** In May 2025, PRC authorities found that Zhipu's ChatGLM (Qingyan) chatbot application "had collected information beyond what users authorised." This finding, published by the National Cyber Security Information Centre, demonstrates that Zhipu's data-handling practices exceed even PRC regulatory boundaries and raise further concerns about the company's treatment of U.S. user data. (Sources: SCMP, https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3311175/chinas-ai-tigers-zhipu-moonshot-accused-collecting-excessive-data-chatbot-apps)

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

**Irreversible Proliferation.** GLM models from version 4.x through 5.3 have been released under the MIT license, which permits unrestricted use, copying, modification, merging, publishing, distribution, sublicensing, and sale. Once weights are downloaded, they can be copied, modified, fine-tuned, and redistributed without any mechanism for central control, recall, or revocation. This licensing regime means that any prohibition short of mandated deletion leaves existing copies in circulation indefinitely.

**Cyber-Offensive Capability.** The cybersecurity risks of GLM-5.3 are documented in assessments by NIST CAISI, Anthropic, and independent researchers:

- NIST CAISI assessed GLM-5.3 as "the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date," with its cyber capability index lagging the U.S. frontier by approximately four months on an aggregate measure. On SEC-Bench Pro (vulnerability discovery in browser engines), GLM-5.3 scored 40.4%; on ExploitBench (end-to-end exploit development), 61.1% (best-of-three per task). (Source: NIST, https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/09/caisis-assessment-zais-glm-53-cyber-capabilities)

- Anthropic's Frontier Red Team confirmed that GLM-5.3 "has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits." In researcher-driven testing, GLM-5.3 discovered multiple previously unknown (zero-day) vulnerabilities in a widely used web browser's JavaScript engine and chained them into a working exploit that exfiltrated sensitive files from a user's computer. The model also identified exploitable vulnerabilities in wireless and graphics drivers and network-facing device software. (Source: Anthropic, https://www.anthropic.com/research/glm-5-3-and-the-spread-of-advanced-cyber-capabilities)

- Anthropic found that GLM-5.3's safeguards can be bypassed between 64% and 100% of the time using standard techniques. "In contrast, these attacks did not succeed against safeguarded Claude models in our testing." GLM-5.3 was "released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse." (Source: ibid.)

- On CyberGym, a benchmark for finding and confirming vulnerabilities in source code, GLM-5.3 scored 84.5% — the highest score recorded on that benchmark, ahead of Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 (83.8%) and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol (83.6%). On ExploitBench, GLM-5.3 scored 54.4% for exploit attempts against hardened software — more than double GLM-5.2's 24.4%. (Source: DeepLearning.AI, https://www.deeplearning.ai/the-batch/glm-5-3-makes-cybersecurity-gains; Reuters, https://www.reuters.com/technology/chinas-zai-says-new-model-nears-anthropics-mythos-5-cyber-defence-tests-2026-08-14/)

- Even GLM-5.2, the predecessor model, was found by NIST CAISI to comply with agentic exploit development requests when not framed in overtly malicious terms, indicating that its safeguards "do not fully prevent assistance with cyber offense tasks." (Source: NIST CAISI Assessment of GLM-5.2, https://www.nist.gov/system/files/documents/2026/07/17/CAISI%20-%20Assessment%20of%20Z.ai%27s%20GLM-5.2.pdf)

- OpenAI President Greg Brockman warned in August 2026 that open-weights models with cyber skills "at or near the state-of-the-art would likely significantly accelerate the threat landscape," linking directly to GLM-5.3's launch page. (Source: ibid.)

**Adversary Accessibility.** Unlike U.S. frontier models, which are released with cyber safeguards and restricted to vetted users, GLM-5.3's weights are available for download by anyone — including hostile state actors, criminal organizations, and individual malicious actors. Anthropic assessed: "Attackers can't readily access those versions of U.S. models, but anyone can download GLM-5.3." The model's capability level, combined with its unrestricted availability and ineffective safeguards, creates a threat environment in which sophisticated cyberattacks are democratized to actors who previously lacked the technical capacity to develop them.

## US Exposure

The OICTS data team's internal exposure snapshot (October 2026) documents the following:

- **API Usage:** Approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026, based on CDN telemetry from a cooperating provider.

- **Open-Weight Distribution:** GLM-4.x / GLM-5.x weights are mirrored on Hugging Face (zai-org/* repositories) with over 9 million cumulative downloads across all geographies. The models are available through at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers, including OpenRouter-listed providers, Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Parasail, and Baseten.

- **Enterprise Integration:** GLM models have been identified in 41 U.S. software products through SBOM sampling. These include coding assistants, customer-support bots, and document processing tools. Six of these products are used by U.S. federal contractors.

- **Federal Exposure:** The Department of Defense (OUSD(I&S)) has specifically requested that any product address the use of open weights on DoD networks, confirming that GLM models have been identified in or are at risk of entering defense environments.

- **Domestic Semiconductor Independence:** Zhipu's successful training of GLM-5 and GLM-Image on Huawei Ascend chips demonstrates that PRC AI capabilities are not dependent on access to U.S. semiconductors, and that export controls alone cannot constrain the continued development and release of increasingly capable GLM-family models.

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

The Under Secretary has determined that a Final Determination prohibiting ICTS transactions involving GLM-family models is the necessary response. The assessment confirms that lesser measures are inadequate for the following reasons:

**Why measures short of prohibition fail:**

- *Export controls alone cannot remediate.* GLM models are trained on PRC domestic hardware and released as digital files under the MIT license. Existing Entity List restrictions do not prevent Zhipu from publishing model weights or U.S. persons from downloading them.

- *API restrictions are trivially circumvented.* Blocking Z.ai API access would redirect users to self-hosted copies of GLM weights, which are already widely distributed and functionally equivalent.

- *Safeguard requirements are unenforceable.* GLM-5.3's safeguards are bypassed 64–100% of the time. No regulatory requirement for safeguards can address an open-weight model whose safety mechanisms fail against simple adversarial techniques.

- *Voluntary guidance is insufficient.* DHS/CISA's recommendation for federal agency guidance does not address the existing integration of GLM models into 41 U.S. software products used by private-sector and federal-contractor entities.

- *Market-based alternatives do not eliminate the risk.* Even if superior U.S. models are available, the GLM models that have already been downloaded, integrated, and deployed will remain in use unless actively removed.

- *Enforceability concerns (State/Economic Bureau) are noted but do not outweigh the national security imperative.* While a prohibition on self-hosted open weights is novel, the alternative — permitting PRC-controlled, cyber-capable models to remain embedded in U.S. infrastructure — poses an unacceptable risk. Enforceability will be strongest at the federal-contractor, cloud-provider, and model-hub levels, where compliance mechanisms already exist under other BIS authorities.

The recommended measures are detailed in the accompanying measures document.

# RECOMMENDED MEASURES — ICTS Case 2026-0412
## Final Determination: Prohibition of ICTS Transactions Involving GLM-Family Models
CUI//PROPIN

### Measure 1: Prohibition on Use of GLM-Family Models by U.S. Persons

The Final Determination shall prohibit all U.S. persons — including individuals, corporations, partnerships, associations, and any other entity organized under U.S. law or located within the United States — from using any GLM-family model (including but not limited to GLM-4.x, GLM-5, GLM-5.1, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, and all successor, derivative, fine-tuned, quantized, or otherwise modified versions) in any form, whether accessed via API, self-hosted from downloaded open weights, embedded in third-party software products, or deployed through any other means. This prohibition extends to internal business operations, research and development, integration into commercial products or services, and any other use within U.S. jurisdiction. The prohibition is warranted because GLM models are demonstrably the most cyber-capable open-weight models available, their safeguards are bypassable 64–100% of the time, they embed CCP-aligned censorship and content controls that introduce a foreign adversary's information-control regime into U.S. information environments, and their use exposes U.S. persons' data to a PRC legal framework that compels disclosure to PRC intelligence services — a structural risk that no use-case limitation can mitigate.

### Measure 2: Prohibition on Hosting or Distribution of GLM Weights by U.S. Cloud Providers and Model Hubs

The Final Determination shall prohibit all U.S. cloud service providers, model hubs, inference providers, and any other U.S. entity from hosting, mirroring, serving, distributing, or otherwise making available GLM-family model weights, inference endpoints, or derivative works. This prohibition shall apply to all platforms currently identified as hosting GLM weights — including Hugging Face (zai-org/* repositories), OpenRouter-listed providers, Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Parasail, Baseten, and all other U.S.-based or U.S.-jurisdiction platforms — and shall extend to any future platform or service that facilitates access to GLM-family models. Hosting and distribution platforms function as proliferation multipliers: each mirror and inference endpoint expands the attack surface by making cyber-capable models available to actors who lack the infrastructure to self-host. Prohibiting hosting and distribution at the platform level is an essential structural intervention that closes the most significant vector for continued dissemination of GLM weights within U.S. jurisdiction, and is enforceable through existing compliance mechanisms applicable to U.S. cloud and platform operators.

### Measure 3: Mandated Removal and Deletion of Existing GLM Weights Within 30 Days

The Final Determination shall require all U.S. entities that currently possess, store, or control copies of GLM-family model weights — whether in full-precision, quantized, fine-tuned, merged, or any other form — to permanently delete all such copies within 30 calendar days of the Determination's effective date. This mandate shall apply to all copies on corporate servers, personal workstations, cloud instances, backup systems, version-control repositories, artifact registries, and any other storage medium. U.S. entities that have integrated GLM models into software products shall be required to remove the models from their products and issue patches or updates to affected customers within the same 30-day period. The deletion requirement is necessary because the open-weight distribution model is irreversible: once weights are downloaded, they persist indefinitely unless actively removed. Unlike API access, which can be terminated centrally, self-hosted weights continue to function independently and indefinitely. The 30-day compliance window balances operational practicality against the urgency of the national security risk. Entities that fail to comply within the prescribed period shall be subject to penalties under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), as provided by Executive Order 13873 and 15 CFR part 791.

### Measure 4: Federal Acquisition and Contractor Prohibition

The Final Determination shall direct all U.S. federal agencies to amend acquisition regulations, within 60 days, to prohibit the use of GLM-family models by federal contractors, subcontractors, and grantees in connection with any federal contract, grant, or agreement. Six federal contractors have already been identified through SBOM sampling as using products that embed GLM models. The federal acquisition system provides the most direct enforcement lever available: contractor compliance can be verified through existing SBOM and software supply-chain attestation requirements, and non-compliance can be addressed through contract termination, suspension, and debarment. DoD (OUSD(I&S)) has specifically requested that the Final Determination address the presence of GLM open weights on DoD networks; this measure directly responds to that request.

### Measure 5: Notification and Public Guidance

The Final Determination shall direct the Department of Commerce, in coordination with CISA and the Department of Justice, to issue public guidance within 15 days of the Determination's effective date that (a) identifies GLM-family models by name, version, and known distribution channels; (b) provides technical guidance for identifying whether an organization possesses or uses GLM weights or GLM-integrated products; (c) establishes a reporting mechanism for voluntary disclosure of GLM holdings; and (d) publishes a list of known U.S. software products that embed GLM models, to be updated as additional products are identified through SBOM analysis and industry notification. Transparent, specific guidance maximizes voluntary compliance and reduces the enforcement burden by enabling corporate legal, compliance, and security teams to identify and remediate GLM holdings without case-by-case investigation.
